sections.title: Seizures, Status Epilepticus and Epileptic Encephalopathies

modules.title: Pediatric Epilepsy Syndromes and Status Epilepticus

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Status Epilepticus: Timelines and Evidence-Based Management

mustKnow.term: ILAE operational definition t1 and t2
mustKnow.fact: ILAE defines status epilepticus by two operational time points: t1 (5 minutes for convulsive status, time to initiate treatment) and t2 (30 minutes, time when long-term neuronal injury and pharmacoresistance ensue).
Initial therapy at 5-10 minutes is a rapid-acting benzodiazepine: IV lorazepam (0.1 mg/kg, max 4 mg), IV diazepam (0.2 mg/kg), or buccal/IM midazolam (0.2 mg/kg, max 10 mg) if IV access is delayed.
The ESETT trial demonstrated equal 50% efficacy between IV levetiracetam (60 mg/kg, max 4500 mg), fosphenytoin (20 mg PE/kg, max 1500 mg PE), and sodium valproate (40 mg/kg, max 3000 mg).
Status epilepticus persisting despite adequate doses of a first-line benzodiazepine and a second-line anti-seizure medication defines Refractory Status Epilepticus (RSE).
Third-line RSE therapy requires continuous anesthetic infusion (midazolam 0.1-2 mg/kg/hr, pentobarbital, or ketamine) with continuous EEG monitoring targeting burst suppression for 24-48 hours.

Propofol is strictly contraindicated for prolonged infusion (> 48 hours or > 4 mg/kg/hr) in young children due to PRIS: metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, and refractory cardiac arrest.

New-Onset Refractory Status Epilepticus (NORSE) and Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) represent neuroinflammatory encephalopathies treated with anakinra, tocilizumab, and ketogenic diet.
In neonates and infants under 1 year with cryptogenic or refractory status, intravenous pyridoxine (100 mg IV under continuous EEG) is administered to treat ALDH7A1 mutations.

lessonTopics.title: West Syndrome and Epileptic Spasms: Diagnosis and Treatment

mustKnow.fact: West syndrome encompasses the triad of epileptic spasms (flexor, extensor, or mixed clusters), hypsarrhythmia on interictal EEG, and developmental arrest or regression.
Epileptic spasms typically begin between 3 and 8 months of age (peak 4-6 months), occurring predominantly upon awakening or during transitional sleep states.
Classic hypsarrhythmia features high-voltage (> 200-300 mcV), chaotic, disorganized background rhythm with multifocal spikes, sharp waves, and absent normal background architecture.
Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH: high-dose 150 IU/m2/day or low-dose 20-30 IU/day for 2 weeks, then tapered) or high-dose oral prednisolone (4-8 mg/kg/day) is first-line therapy.
Vigabatrin (100-150 mg/kg/day) is the definitive drug of choice for epileptic spasms secondary to Tuberous Sclerosis Complex, achieving spasm cessation in over 80%.
Vigabatrin causes irreversible, bilateral concentric visual field constriction in 30-40% of treated children, requiring electroretinogram (ERG) or perimetry monitoring every 3 months.
Rapid cessation of clinical spasms and complete resolution of hypsarrhythmia within 14 days of initiating therapy is the single strongest predictor of long-term cognitive outcome.
Approximately 20-50% of children with untreated or refractory West syndrome progress into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in later childhood.

lessonTopics.title: Dravet Syndrome: Genetics, Triggers and Drug Contraindications

mustKnow.fact: Over 80-85% of Dravet syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy) cases are caused by de novo loss-of-function mutations in SCN1A encoding the Nav1.1 sodium channel alpha subunit.
Onset occurs in the first year of life (peak 5-8 months) as prolonged febrile or afebrile hemiclonic or generalized clonic status epilepticus in a previously normal infant.
Seizures are characteristically provoked by modest body temperature elevation (fever, warm bath, exercise) and visual patterns (flickering light, visual patterns).

Sodium channel-blocking anti-seizure medications (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, vigabatrin) are strictly contraindicated because they aggravate seizures and precipitate status.
First-line maintenance treatment combines clobazam (0.5-1 mg/kg/day) and sodium valproate (20-40 mg/kg/day).
Stiripentol (50 mg/kg/day) added to clobazam and valproate acts via GABAergic enhancement and CYP450 inhibition, reducing prolonged seizures by > 70%.
Fenfluramine (0.2-0.7 mg/kg/day) provides marked seizure reduction via sigma-1 receptor and 5-HT2 serotonergic modulation; requires echocardiographic monitoring for cardiac valvulopathy.
Cannabidiol (purified CBD 10-20 mg/kg/day) significantly reduces convulsive seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome, requiring baseline serum transaminase monitoring.

lessonTopics.title: Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome and Atonic Seizures

mustKnow.fact: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is defined by: multiple intractable seizure types (tonic, atonic drop attacks, atypical absence), slow spike-and-wave EEG (< 2.5 Hz), and progressive intellectual impairment.
Tonic seizures occurring during non-REM sleep accompanied by generalized paroxysmal fast activity (GPFA, 10-20 Hz) on polysomnography/EEG are the neurophysiological hallmark of LGS.
Sudden loss of postural tone produces catastrophic fall injuries, mandating protective helmet use with faceguard in ambulatory patients.
First-line therapy combines sodium valproate (20-40 mg/kg/day) with clobazam (0.5-1 mg/kg/day) or lamotrigine (slowly titrated to prevent Stevens-Johnson syndrome).
Rufinamide (10-45 mg/kg/day) is specifically approved as adjunctive therapy for drop attacks and tonic-atonic seizures in LGS patients aged 1 year and older.
Felbamate is highly effective for refractory LGS but carries black-box warnings for aplastic anemia (1 in 4,000) and fatal acute hepatic necrosis, requiring biweekly complete blood count monitoring.
A 4:1 or 3:1 lipid-to-non-lipid classic ketogenic diet achieves > 50% seizure reduction in over 40-50% of children with drug-resistant LGS.
Anterior two-thirds or complete corpus callosotomy prevents interhemispheric propagation of epileptic discharges, reducing atonic drop attacks by > 70-80% in non-resectable LGS.

lessonTopics.title: Childhood Absence Epilepsy and Self-Limited Focal Epilepsies

mustKnow.fact: Childhood Absence Epilepsy (CAE) pathognomonic EEG demonstrates synchronous, generalized, symmetrical 3 Hz (2.5-3.5 Hz) spike-and-wave complexes on a normal background.
Hyperventilation for 3 minutes reliably provokes clinical absence seizures with synchronous 3 Hz discharges in over 90% of untreated patients in the clinic.
Ethosuximide (15-40 mg/kg/day) is the first-line drug of choice for CAE, matching valproate in efficacy but with significantly fewer attentional and cognitive adverse effects (NIH trial).
Sodium valproate is the preferred alternative when absence seizures coexist with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, as ethosuximide does not protect against convulsive seizures.
Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS / rolandic) features nocturnal hemifacial clonic twitches, gurgling, and salivation with broad centrotemporal sharp waves on sleep EEG.
Many children with SeLECTS require no treatment; when frequent or daytime seizures occur, sulthiame (5 mg/kg/day) or levetiracetam (20-30 mg/kg/day) is preferred.
Self-limited focal epilepsy with autonomic seizures features prolonged episodes of pallor, nausea, vomiting, pupillary dilation, and behavioral arrest, with shifting multifocal occipital spikes.
Both CAE and SeLECTS have excellent prognoses, with spontaneous complete remission occurring in over 90-95% of patients by mid-adolescence (age 12-15 years).

sections.title: Neuromuscular Disorders and Motor Neuron Diseases

modules.title: Spinal Muscular Atrophy, Duchenne Dystrophy and Neuropathies

lessonTopics.title: Spinal Muscular Atrophy: SMN Genetics, Subtypes and Disease-Modifying Therapies

mustKnow.fact: Over 95% of SMA cases are caused by homozygous deletion of exon 7 (or exons 7 and 8) in the survival motor neuron 1 (SMN1) gene located on chromosome 5q13.
The SMN2 gene has a C-to-T transition in exon 7 causing exon 7 exclusion in 90% of transcripts; higher SMN2 copy numbers (3 or 4 copies) produce milder clinical phenotypes.
SMA Type 1 (onset < 6 months) presents with severe hypotonia (floppy infant), absent deep tendon reflexes, tongue fasciculations, bell-shaped thorax with paradoxical breathing, and inability to sit.
SMA Type 2 (onset 6-18 months) achieves sitting unsupported but never walks independently; Type 3 (Kugelberg-Welander, onset > 18 months) achieves unassisted ambulation.
Nusinersen (Spinraza) is an intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide modifying SMN2 pre-mRNA splicing to promote full-length SMN protein inclusion, dosed via loading then every 4 months.
Onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma) delivers an AAV9 vector carrying cDNA encoding human SMN protein via a single intravenous infusion (1.1 x 10^14 vg/kg) in children < 2 years.
Risdiplam (Evrysdi) is an orally administered small molecule SMN2 splicing modifier taken daily with food, approved for infants from birth upwards.
Oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) is mandatory starting 24 hours prior to onasemnogene infusion and continued for at least 30 days to mitigate acute immune hepatotoxicity and troponin elevation.

lessonTopics.title: Duchenne and Becker Muscular Dystrophies: Dystrophinopathy Management

mustKnow.fact: DMD is caused by out-of-frame deletions (60-70%) or duplications in the DMD gene on Xp21.2, resulting in complete absence of functional dystrophin protein (< 5% on muscle biopsy).
Serum creatine kinase (CK) is massively elevated at 10 to 100 times the upper reference limit (> 10,000-50,000 U/L) from birth, even prior to overt clinical weakness.
Boys present between 3 and 5 years with proximal lower limb weakness, climbing up their legs to stand (Gowers sign), waddling gait, and calf pseudohypertrophy (fibroadipose replacement).
Prednisone (0.75 mg/kg/day) or deflazacort (0.9 mg/kg/day) starting at age 4-6 prolongs independent ambulation by 2-3 years, preserves upper body strength, and delays scoliosis and cardiomyopathy.

Phosphorodiamidate morpholino antisense oligonucleotides restore the reading frame: eteplirsen skips exon 51 (13% of DMD), golodirsen and viltolarsen skip exon 53 (8% of DMD), and casimersen skips exon 45.
Dystrophic dilated cardiomyopathy develops in nearly all boys by late adolescence; annual cardiac MRI/echo and prophylactic ACE inhibitor therapy (perindopril or enalapril) are initiated by age 10.

Forced vital capacity (FVC) monitoring is essential; initiation of nocturnal non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP) is indicated when FVC drops below 50% predicted or sleep hypoventilation occurs.
Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD) involves in-frame DMD deletions producing a truncated but partially functional dystrophin protein, with ambulation preserved beyond 16 years of age.

lessonTopics.title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome and Juvenile Myasthenia Gravis

mustKnow.fact: GBS is an acute post-infectious polyradiculoneuropathy featuring symmetrical ascending flaccid quadriparesis, hyporeflexia or areflexia, and variable autonomic instability.
CSF classically demonstrates elevated protein (> 45 mg/dL) with normal white blood cell count (< 5-10 mononuclear cells/mcL), with protein elevation peaking at 2 to 4 weeks.

Campylobacter jejuni enteritis is the most frequent trigger, associated with AMAN and molecular mimicry against GM1/GD1a gangliosides; Miller Fisher syndrome (GQ1b antibodies) features triad of ataxia, areflexia, and ophthalmoplegia.
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 2 g/kg total, given as 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days or 1 g/kg/day for 2 days) or plasmapheresis is first-line; systemic corticosteroids are proven ineffective.

The 20/30/40 rule: vital capacity < 20 mL/kg, maximum inspiratory pressure < 30 cmH2O, or maximum expiratory pressure < 40 cmH2O indicates impending diaphragmatic paralysis requiring mechanical ventilation.
Autoantibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (AChR-Ab) are positive in 70-80% of generalized juvenile myasthenia, with anti-MuSK antibodies found in up to 40% of seronegative cases.
Oral acetylcholinesterase inhibitor pyridostigmine (0.5-1 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 300 mg/day) provides symptomatic improvement without modifying underlying autoimmunity.
Thymectomy significantly improves remission rates and reduces corticosteroid dose requirements in post-pubertal AChR-positive generalized myasthenia gravis.

lessonTopics.title: Hypotonic Floppy Infant: Central vs Peripheral Localization and Workup

mustKnow.fact: Central hypotonia (80% of floppy infants) features axial weakness greater than limb weakness, brisk or normal deep tendon reflexes, clonus, fisting, and dysmorphism, whereas peripheral hypotonia features profound antigravity weakness, absent reflexes, and frog-leg posture.

On pull-to-sit (traction response), complete head lag past 4 months is abnormal; on vertical suspension, slipping through examiner hands indicates shoulder girdle weakness (classic peripheral hypotonia).
Normal infants suspend convexly with head held up and limbs flexed; floppy infants hang like an inverted U over the examiner hand.

mustKnow.term: Anterior horn cell clues in floppy neonate
mustKnow.fact: Fasciculations of the tongue, bell-shaped chest, diaphragmatic respiration, and complete areflexia in an alert neonate strongly indicate SMA type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann).

Prader-Willi syndrome presents with severe neonatal hypotonia, cryptorchidism, hypogonadism, and poor suck, diagnosed by 15q11-q13 methylation-specific PCR (maternal uniparental disomy or paternal deletion).

Congenital myasthenia (muscle weakness fatiguing with activity) responds to pyridostigmine or 3,4-DAP; congenital myotonic dystrophy presents with severe hypotonia, tented upper lip (carp mouth), and maternal history of grip myotonia.
Initial workup of unexplained neonatal hypotonia includes blood gas (metabolic acidosis), lactate, pyruvate, serum creatine kinase (CK), ammonia, and acylcarnitine profile.

Infant botulism presents at 2-6 months with acute descending paralysis, constipation, pupillary unresponsiveness, and weak cry following honey ingestion or soil exposure, treated with Botulism Immune Globulin Intravenous (BabyBIG).

lessonTopics.title: Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease and Hereditary Neuropathies in Children

mustKnow.fact: CMT1A represents 70-80% of demyelinating hereditary neuropathies and is caused by a 1.4 Mb duplication of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17p11.2.
Median motor nerve conduction velocity distinguishes CMT1 (demyelinating, NCV < 38 m/s, often 15-25 m/s) from CMT2 (axonal, NCV > 38 m/s with reduced compound muscle action potential amplitudes).

mustKnow.term: Stork leg and inverted champagne bottle appearance
mustKnow.fact: Distal muscle wasting predominantly affecting the peroneus, anterior tibial, and calf muscles leads to inverted champagne bottle appearance with bilateral pes cavus and hammer toes.

X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1 (CMTX1) is caused by mutations in the connexin-32 gene (GJB1) on chromosome Xq13.1, causing intermediate NCV (30-45 m/s) and transient stroke-like episodes during altitude or fever.

Hereditary Neuropathy with Liability to Pressure Palsies (HNPP) results from a 1.4 Mb deletion of PMP22 on 17p11.2, presenting with recurrent painless focal compressive neuropathies (peroneal, radial, ulnar) and sausage-like tomacula on nerve biopsy.

Dejerine-Sottas is a severe congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy manifesting in infancy with delayed motor milestones, severe ataxia, palpable thickened nerves, onion-bulb formations, and motor NCV < 10 m/s.

Vincristine is strictly contraindicated in patients with CMT due to precipitous and irreversible axonal neuropathy; other neurotoxic agents like paclitaxel, nitrofurantoin, and metronidazole must be avoided.

Early ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs) prevent Achilles tendon contractures; surgical interventions include plantar fascia release, tendon transfers (posterior tibial tendon to dorsum), and calcaneal osteotomy.

lessonTopics.title: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM) and MOGAD

mustKnow.fact: IPMSSG defines ADEM by: acute encephalopathy (lethargy, irritability, or coma) not explained by fever, multifocal neurological deficits, and neuroimaging showing fluffy demyelinating white matter lesions.

Brain MRI demonstrates bilateral, asymmetrical, large, fluffy, poorly marginated hyperintense lesions on T2/FLAIR predominantly involving subcortical and deep white matter, thalami, and basal ganglia.
Antibodies to myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG-IgG) are detected in 40-50% of children presenting with acute ADEM, correlating with younger age and lower risk of MS conversion.
Intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy (30 mg/kg/day, maximum 1000 mg/day for 3 to 5 days) followed by an oral prednisolone taper over 4-6 weeks is the gold standard induction.

mustKnow.term: Second-line rescue with IVIG or PLEX
mustKnow.fact: In patients with inadequate response after 3-5 days of high-dose steroids, IVIG (2 g/kg total over 2 days) or therapeutic plasma exchange (5-7 exchanges) is initiated.

NMOSD is defined by serum Aquaporin-4 (AQP4-IgG) autoantibodies targeting astrocytic water channels, presenting with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM >= 3 vertebral segments) and bilateral optic neuritis.
ADEM is classically monophasic; a subsequent demyelinating attack separated by at least 3 months from onset defines multiphasic ADEM or heralds conversion to MOGAD or multiple sclerosis.
Pediatric MS requires dissemination in space and time; CSF-restricted oligoclonal IgG bands (OCBs) are present in 80-90% of pediatric MS but are negative in > 85% of MOGAD cases.

lessonTopics.title: Anti-NMDAR Encephalitis and Pediatric Autoimmune Encephalitis

mustKnow.fact: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) encephalitis is the most common autoimmune encephalitis in children, targeting the GluN1 subunit of the receptor.

Illness progresses through characteristic stages: prodromal viral-like phase, acute behavioral/psychiatric changes (agitation, hallucinations), catatonia, speech regression, seizures, and severe autonomic instability with hypoventilation.
Bizarre, involuntary stereotypic movements including oral-lingual chewing, lip-smacking, grimacing, choreoathetosis, and oculogyric crises are pathognomonic hallmarks.
Continuous EEG demonstrates the extreme delta brush pattern (rhythmic beta frequency activity superimposed on rhythmic delta waves) in approximately 30% of pediatric cases.
Coexisting ovarian mature cystic teratoma is found in over 50% of adult female patients but in under 10% of prepubertal girls with anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
First-line therapy combines high-dose IV methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day for 5 days) alongside intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg) or therapeutic plasma exchange.
Failure of clinical improvement within 10-14 days mandates second-line therapy with rituximab (anti-CD20, 375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses) and/or cyclophosphamide.
Up to 25% of children recovering from Herpes Simplex Virus encephalitis develop secondary anti-NMDAR encephalitis 2 to 8 weeks post-infection due to exposed neuronal antigens.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Bacterial Meningitis: Pathogens, CSF Interpretation and Complications

mustKnow.fact: In neonates < 1 month, Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria monocytogenes predominate; beyond 1 month, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis account for over 85% of cases.
Typical bacterial meningitis CSF reveals neutrophilic pleocytosis (> 1000/mm³), elevated protein (> 100-500 mg/dL), and CSF to serum glucose ratio < 0.4 (or absolute CSF glucose < 40 mg/dL).

Empiric therapy in infants and children is ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/day IV divided q12h, max 4 g) or cefotaxime plus vancomycin (60 mg/kg/day divided q6h) to cover cephalosporin-resistant S. pneumoniae.

Intravenous dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg q6h for 2-4 days) must be given prior to or with the first dose of antibiotics in proven or suspected H. influenzae type b or S. pneumoniae to reduce sensorineural hearing loss.
Sensorineural hearing loss occurs in 10-30% of pneumococcal meningitis survivors due to suppurative labyrinthitis and cochlear ossification, mandating formal audiometry prior to hospital discharge.

Subdural effusion occurs in 50% of infants with H. influenzae or pneumococcal meningitis and requires observation unless causing focal deficits or mass effect; subdural empyema requires urgent surgical drainage and 4-6 weeks of parenteral antibiotics.
Lumbar puncture should be preceded by head CT only if focal neurological deficits, new onset seizures, persistent coma, or signs of raised ICP (papilledema, bradycardia, hypertension) are present.

Household contacts of Neisseria meningitidis require rifampin (10 mg/kg PO q12h for 2 days), ciprofloxacin (single 500 mg dose), or ceftriaxone (single 125-250 mg IM dose); H. influenzae contacts require rifampin 20 mg/kg once daily for 4 days.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Viral Encephalitis: Neonatal and Child HSV, Japanese Encephalitis and Enterovirus A71

mustKnow.fact: Pediatric HSV-1 encephalitis classically affects the frontotemporal lobes and insular cortex, producing periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) on EEG.

mustKnow.term: Acyclovir dosing and duration in children
mustKnow.fact: Intravenous acyclovir is dosed at 20 mg/kg IV q8h (neonates) for 21 days, or 10-15 mg/kg IV q8h (older children) for 14-21 days, followed by oral suppressive acyclovir for 6 months in neonates to improve neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Secondary choreoathetosis and cognitive deterioration 2-6 weeks following treated HSV encephalitis is caused by autoimmune anti-NMDAR antibodies in up to 25% of cases.
Japanese encephalitis virus has selective tropism for the bilateral thalami, basal ganglia, and brainstem, presenting with parkinsonian tremors, masked facies, and cogwheel rigidity.

mustKnow.term: JE diagnosis via IgM capture ELISA
mustKnow.fact: Confirmation of Japanese encephalitis requires detection of JE-specific IgM in CSF or serum via MAC-ELISA; no specific antiviral therapy exists, management is neurocritical support.
Enterovirus A71 causes hand-foot-and-mouth disease complicated by severe rhombencephalitis, neurogenic pulmonary edema, tachycardia, and sudden autonomic storm with high mortality.
CSF HSV PCR may yield false negatives within the first 24-48 hours of illness; if suspicion is high, continue IV acyclovir and repeat CSF PCR at 3-7 days.
ANEC is triggered by influenza or HHV-6 in children with RANBP2 mutations, producing rapid coma, seizures, and symmetric tricolor lesions in the bilateral thalami on brain MRI.

modules.title: Pediatric Stroke, Moyamoya and Movement Disorders

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Arterial Ischemic Stroke and Moyamoya Arteriopathy

mustKnow.fact: Pediatric arterial ischemic stroke (AIS) occurs in 2-3 per 100,000 children per year, with median diagnosis delay exceeding 20-24 hours due to under-recognition of acute focal hemiparesis.
Focal Cerebral Arteriopathy (FCA) / post-varicella arteriopathy is the leading cause of arterial stroke in previously healthy children, causing unilateral irregular stenosis of the proximal MCA/ACA.
Transcranial Doppler (TCD) screening of time-averaged mean maximum velocity in terminal ICA/MCA: >= 200 cm/s indicates high stroke risk (STOP trial), treated with chronic blood transfusion.
Initial therapy for confirmed pediatric AIS (without hemorrhage) is unfractionated heparin or low molecular weight heparin (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 12 hr), transitioning to aspirin (3-5 mg/kg/day).
Moyamoya disease features bilateral progressive stenosis/occlusion of the supraclinoid internal carotid arteries with hazy network of lenticulostriate collaterals (puff of smoke / moyamoya).
The p.R4810K polymorphism in the ring finger protein 213 (RNF213) gene is the major genetic susceptibility factor for moyamoya disease in East Asian populations.

Indirect surgical revascularization (encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis / EDAS or pial synangiosis) induces neocollateral sprouting from external to internal carotid territories, reducing stroke recurrence by > 80%.

CSVT manifests with seizures and elevated ICP associated with mastoiditis, dehydration, or prothrombotic mutations, treated with anticoagulation (LMWH) for 3 to 6 months even with secondary hemorrhagic infarction.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Movement Disorders, Tics and Acute Ataxia

mustKnow.fact: Acute cerebellitis is the most common cause of acute ataxia in toddlers (aged 2-5 years), presenting with sudden truncal ataxia and titubation 1-3 weeks following varicella or Epstein-Barr virus.
Kinsbourne dancing eyes syndrome features chaotic saccadic eye movements (opsoclonus), myoclonus, and ataxia; over 50% of pediatric cases are paraneoplastic due to occult occult neuroblastoma.
DSM-5 Tourette syndrome requires both multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic present for more than 1 year, with onset before 18 years of age and not attributable to substance use.
CBIT (habit reversal therapy) is the first-line non-pharmacological treatment of choice; alpha-2 adrenergic agonists (clonidine, guanfacine) are first-line medications.

Segawa disease (GCH1 gene mutation causing GTP cyclohydrolase 1 deficiency) features diurnal worsening of foot dystonia and parkinsonism, demonstrating dramatic, sustained response to low-dose levodopa.
Autosomal recessive ATM mutation features progressive cerebellar ataxia starting in toddlerhood, oculocutaneous telangiectasias by age 3-5, elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), and IgA deficiency.

Friedreich ataxia is caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the FXN gene (frataxin deficiency), featuring sensory ataxia, absent ankle reflexes, extensor plantars, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and diabetes.
Sydenham chorea manifests with rapid, purposeless, jerky movements, piano-playing sign (involuntary finger fasciculations on arm extension), and milkmaid grip (fluctuating grip strength).

modules.title: Leukodystrophies, Neurometabolic Crises and Mitochondrial Disease

lessonTopics.title: Metachromatic Leukodystrophy, X-ALD, Krabbe and Canavan Disease

mustKnow.fact: MLD is caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency leading to cerebroside sulfate (sulfatide) accumulation in lysosomes, featuring symmetric confluent periventricular T2 hyperintensity with sparing of subcortical U-fibers.
Spared radiating myelinated fibers along perivenular spaces in MLD produce the pathognomonic tigroid or leopard-skin appearance on axial T2-weighted MRI.

X-ALD is caused by ABCD1 peroxisomal transporter mutations causing accumulation of Very Long Chain Fatty Acids (VLCFA, C26:0 and C26:1), presenting in school-age boys with behavioral decline and adrenal insufficiency.

mustKnow.term: Loes score and MRI zones in X-ALD
mustKnow.fact: X-ALD classically starts in the splenium of the corpus callosum and parieto-occipital white matter, displaying three characteristic zones on T2 MRI with an actively enhancing intermediate inflammatory zone.

Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy) results from galactocerebrosidase (GALC) deficiency, presenting in early infancy with extreme irritability, hyperesthesia, optic atrophy, and CT hyperdensity in thalami.

Canavan disease (aspartoacylase deficiency) leads to high N-acetylaspartate (NAA) in brain and urine, producing macrocephaly and massive prominent NAA peak on MR spectroscopy with diffuse spongy myelin degeneration involving U-fibers.
Alexander disease (GFAP gain-of-function mutation in astrocytes) features severe frontal lobe white matter T2 hyperintensity, Rosenthal fibers on histopathology, and macrocephaly.
PLP1 mutation causes PMD, a permanent hypomyelinating leukodystrophy characterized by pendular nystagmus from early infancy, ataxia, and diffuse arrest of normal T1/T2 white matter myelination.

lessonTopics.title: Mitochondrial Encephalopathies: Leigh Syndrome and MELAS

mustKnow.fact: Leigh syndrome (subacute necrotizing encephalomyelopathy) features symmetrical, bilateral T2-hyperintense necrotic lesions in the basal ganglia (putamina), periaqueductal gray, and brainstem.
Persistent lactic acidosis with elevated CSF lactate and a prominent double inverted lactate doublet at 1.33 ppm on MR spectroscopy is characteristic of mitochondrial respiratory chain defects.
Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes (MELAS) is driven by the m.3243A>G mutation in the MT-TL1 mitochondrial tRNA gene in over 80% of patients.
Stroke-like episodes in MELAS produce cortical and subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities that cross anatomical arterial vascular territories, typically affecting the parietal and occipital lobes.
Intravenous L-arginine infusion (0.5 g/kg during acute stroke-like episode, followed by oral maintenance) restores nitric oxide-mediated microvascular perfusion and accelerates recovery in MELAS.
Sodium valproate is strictly contraindicated in suspected mitochondrial disease with POLG mutations (Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome) due to high risk of precipitating fulminant fatal hepatic necrosis.

Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibers (MERRF, m.8344A>G mutation) demonstrates accumulation of abnormal subsarcolemmal mitochondria visible as ragged red fibers on modified Gomori trichrome stain.

SLC19A3 mutation causes biotin-thiamine responsive basal ganglia disease, presenting with subacute encephalopathy and bilateral caudate/putamen necrosis, reversed completely by high-dose biotin and thiamine.

lessonTopics.title: Neurofibromatosis Type 1 and Tuberous Sclerosis Complex: Clinical Criteria and Therapies

mustKnow.fact: NF1 diagnosis requires >= 2 criteria: >= 6 café-au-lait macules (> 5 mm prepubertal, > 15 mm postpubertal), axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe sign), >= 2 neurofibromas or 1 plexiform, optic pathway glioma, >= 2 Lisch nodules or choroidal abnormalities, sphenoid wing dysplasia / pseudoarthrosis, and heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant.
Selumetinib (oral MEK1/2 inhibitor, 25 mg/m² PO BID) is approved for pediatric inoperable symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas, achieving >= 20% volume reduction in over 70% of patients.

Children with NF1 under 7 years require annual visual acuity and fundus examination to detect optic pathway gliomas (15-20% incidence); first-line chemotherapy if progressive is carboplatin and vincristine.

TSC diagnosis requires 2 major criteria or 1 major plus >= 2 minor criteria; major criteria include >= 3 ash-leaf macules (>= 5 mm), >= 3 angiofibromas or fibrous cephalic plaque, >= 2 ungual fibromas, shagreen patch, cortical tubers, subependymal nodules (SEN), SEGA, cardiac rhabdomyoma, lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), and >= 2 angiomyolipomas.

Subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGA) arise near the foramen of Monro causing hydrocephalus; oral mTOR inhibitors (everolimus 4.5 mg/m²/day targeting trough 5-15 ng/mL) induce tumor regression without surgery.
Cardiac rhabdomyomas are detected in up to 80% of infants with TSC on fetal echocardiography and spontaneously regress in early childhood as maternal estrogen wanes.

mustKnow.term: Epilepsy surveillance and vigabatrin in TSC
mustKnow.fact: Serial EEGs are recommended in asymptomatic infants with TSC; onset of electrographic or clinical spasms warrants immediate first-line treatment with vigabatrin (100-150 mg/kg/day).

Renal ultrasound or MRI every 1-3 years tracks angiomyolipomas; lesions > 3 cm diameter are treated with everolimus or selective embolization to prevent life-threatening retroperitoneal hemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome).

lessonTopics.title: Sturge-Weber Syndrome, Ataxia Telangiectasia and Von Hippel-Lindau Disease

mustKnow.fact: Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by an activating mosaic somatic mutation in GNAQ (p.Arg183Gln) and is characterized by facial port-wine birthmark in the V1 ophthalmic trigeminal distribution, leptomeningeal angioma, and glaucoma.

Brain CT in Sturge-Weber demonstrates gyriform cortical calcification (tram-track sign) beneath the leptomeningeal angiomatosis, associated with progressive cerebral atrophy and refractory focal seizures.

mustKnow.term: Ataxia telangiectasia ATM gene and AFP
mustKnow.fact: Ataxia telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by ATM gene mutations (11q22.3) on DNA double-strand break repair, featuring progressive cerebellar ataxia, ocular telangiectasias, elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP > 10 ng/mL), and radiosensitivity.
Patients with AT exhibit IgA, IgG2, and IgE deficiency with lymphopenia, suffering recurrent sinopulmonary infections and a 100-fold increased risk of lymphoid malignancies (T-cell ALL, lymphoma).

mustKnow.term: Von Hippel-Lindau VHL gene and hemangioblastomas
mustKnow.fact: VHL disease (3p25.3 deletion or mutation) causes retinal and cerebellar capillary hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal carcinoma, and pheochromocytomas due to constitutive HIF-2alpha activation.
Belzutifan (oral HIF-2alpha inhibitor, 120 mg daily in adults/adolescents) is FDA-approved for VHL-associated hemangioblastomas, RCC, and neuroendocrine tumors, sparing repeated resections.

Incontinentia pigmenti is an X-linked dominant IKBKG/NEMO mutation lethal in males, progressing through 4 cutaneous stages: vesicular (neonatal), verrucous (infancy), hyperpigmented whorls along Blaschko lines, and atrophic hypopigmented streaks.

Infants with facial capillary malformation involving the upper eyelid require serial intraocular pressure measurement every 3-6 months to detect congenital glaucoma (present in 30-70% of V1 port-wine stains).

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Brain Tumours: Medulloblastoma, Astrocytomas and Posterior Fossa Masses

mustKnow.fact: Over 50-60% of pediatric brain tumors occur in the posterior fossa (infratentorial) in children aged 1-10 years, most commonly pilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma, and ependymoma.

WHO classifies medulloblastoma into 4 molecular subgroups: WNT (best prognosis, > 95% 5-year survival, CTNNB1 mutation), SHH (TP53 wild-type good, mutated poor), Group 3 (worst prognosis, MYC amplification, leptomeningeal dissemination), and Group 4 (most common, isochromosome 17q).

Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO Grade 1) is cystic with an enhancing mural nodule, characterized by KIAA1549-BRAF gene fusion or BRAF V600E mutation, with excellent > 90% 10-year survival following complete resection.

mustKnow.term: Ependymoma plastic growth and CSF staging
mustKnow.fact: Posterior fossa ependymomas arise from the floor of the fourth ventricle, squeeze through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie (plastic tumor), and require craniospinal axis MRI and lumbar CSF cytology 2 weeks post-op.

Diffuse Intrinsic Pontine Glioma (now Diffuse Midline Glioma H3 K27M-altered, WHO Grade 4) expands the pons, causing triad of multiple cranial neuropathies (VI, VII), long-tract signs, and ataxia, with median survival under 12 months.

Craniospinal irradiation (CSI) is strictly avoided in children < 3 years to prevent devastating neurocognitive and endocrinological deficits; high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell rescue is used instead.

Adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas (CTNNB1 mutations) present with bitemporal hemianopsia, growth failure, and diabetes insipidus, displaying cystic machinery oil fluid and calcification on neuroimaging.

Cerebellar mutism syndrome develops in 25% of children 24-48 hours following posterior fossa tumor resection, featuring loss of speech, emotional lability, ataxia, and hypotonia due to dentato-thalamo-cortical tract disruption.

sections.title: Brain Malformations, Hydrocephalus and Intracranial Pressure

modules.title: Congenital Malformations, Hydrocephalus and Raised ICP

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Hydrocephalus: Etiology, VP Shunts and ETV Management

mustKnow.fact: Non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus results from intraventricular CSF flow block (aqueductal stenosis, Chiari, Dandy-Walker), while communicating hydrocephalus is caused by impaired arachnoid granulation resorption (post-hemorrhagic, post-meningitic).

Infant hydrocephalus presents with accelerated head circumference crossing percentiles, bulging anterior fontanelle, cracked-pot sound on percussion (Macewen sign), and upward gaze paralysis (sun-setting sign) from tectal compression.

mustKnow.term: VP shunt failure timeline and causes
mustKnow.fact: Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunts fail in 30-40% of cases in the first year, most commonly from proximal ventricular catheter obstruction by choroid plexus or debris.

Over 70% of shunt infections occur within 2 months of surgery, caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase-negative staphylococci) and S. aureus, requiring shunt externalization and IV vancomycin.

ETV punctures the tuber cinereum / third ventricle floor into the interpeduncular cistern, indicated in obstructive hydrocephalus; the ETV Success Score incorporates age, etiology, and prior shunt history.
Chronic CSF overdrainage produces collapsed ventricular walls (slit ventricle syndrome), low CSF pressure headaches relieved by lying flat, and recurrent proximal catheter occlusion.

Distal shunt malfunction may present as painless abdominal distension, recurrent fever, or a loculated CSF peritoneal pseudocyst requiring laparoscopic externalization or relocation to pleura (VP to VP/VA shunt).

In premature infants with intraventricular hemorrhage, ventricular reservoirs or subgaleal shunts permit serial CSF tapping (10-15 mL/kg) until the infant reaches 2-2.5 kg weight for definitive shunting.

lessonTopics.title: Neural Tube Defects, Chiari Malformations and Dandy-Walker Continuum

mustKnow.fact: Periconceptional folic acid supplementation (0.4 mg/day for standard risk, 4.0 mg/day for mothers with a previous affected child or on valproate) from 1 month prior to conception through 12 weeks reduces neural tube defects by 70%.
mustKnow.source: CDC / WHO Neural Tube Defect Prevention

mustKnow.fact: The MOMS trial demonstrated that prenatal in-utero repair of myelomeningocele before 26 weeks gestation reduces the need for postnatal hydrocephalus shunting by 50% and improves motor function compared to postnatal repair.

Chiari I malformation is defined as inferior displacement of cerebellar tonsils > 5 mm below the foramen magnum on sagittal MRI, strongly associated with cervical syringomyelia (seen in 50-70% of symptomatic cases).

Chiari II malformation is almost universally associated with open myelomeningocele, featuring downward herniation of cerebellar vermis, fourth ventricle, and medulla into cervical canal with beaked tectum and luckenschadel.

Dandy-Walker malformation is defined by the triad of complete or partial agenesis of the cerebellar vermis, cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle, and an enlarged posterior fossa with elevated tentorium and torcula.

Tethered cord syndrome features low-lying conus medullaris below L2 vertebral body, presenting in growing children with asymmetric leg weakness, progressive scoliosis, neurogenic bladder, and foot deformities.

Neonates with myelomeningocele require early clean intermittent catheterization (CIC q4h) and anticholinergic agents (oxybutynin 0.2 mg/kg/day) to keep detrusor leak point pressure < 40 cmH2O and protect renal function.
Up to 70% of patients with spina bifida develop IgE-mediated latex allergy due to early repeated mucosal exposures; strict latex-free protocol is mandatory from birth for all procedures.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Headaches: Migraine, Tension-Type and Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension

mustKnow.fact: ICHD-3 criteria recognize pediatric migraine as shorter than adults (2-72 hours) and frequently bilateral (frontotemporal) rather than strictly unilateral, with pulsatile quality, photophobia, phonophobia, and nausea.
mustKnow.source: ICHD-3 International Classification of Headache Disorders

mustKnow.term: Triptan licensing in pediatric acute migraine
mustKnow.fact: Nasal sumatriptan (5-20 mg) and zolmitriptan (2.5-5 mg nasal spray) are approved for adolescents >= 12 years; oral rizatriptan (5-10 mg) is approved for children >= 6 years taken at headache onset.

The NIH-funded CHAMP trial showed no statistically significant difference in headache reduction between amitriptyline, topiramate, and placebo in children, emphasizing behavioral therapy, sleep hygiene, and hydration.
Episodic childhood migraine syndromes include abdominal migraine (paroxysmal midline abdominal pain with vasomotor changes) and cyclic vomiting syndrome, responding to cyproheptadine or pizotifen.

Definite IIH requires papilledema, normal neurological examination except 6th nerve palsy, normal neuroimaging (empty sella, optic nerve sheath flattening), normal CSF composition, and elevated opening pressure >= 28 cmH2O.
First-line medical therapy for pediatric IIH is oral acetazolamide (20-100 mg/kg/day divided TID, max 2-4 g/day) to inhibit choroid plexus carbonic anhydrase and reduce CSF formation.

mustKnow.term: Secondary causes of raised ICP without mass
mustKnow.fact: Pediatric pseudotumor cerebri triggers include tetracyclines (minocycline, doxycycline), excess or withdrawal of corticosteroids, hypervitaminosis A (isotretinoin), growth hormone therapy, and venous sinus thrombosis.

mustKnow.term: Optic nerve sheath fenestration vs shunting
mustKnow.fact: In patients with progressive visual field constriction or failing vision despite maximum acetazolamide, urgent optic nerve sheath fenestration or lumboperitoneal / ventriculoperitoneal shunting is required to preserve vision.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Traumatic Brain Injury: Raised ICP, Monroe-Kellie and Tiered Management

mustKnow.fact: PECARN criteria identify children at very low risk (< 0.05%) of clinically important traumatic brain injury (ciTBI), safely avoiding CT in children >= 2 years with GCS 15, no LOC, normal behavior, and no basilar skull fracture signs.

Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP - ICP) targets in pediatric severe TBI are age-dependent: 40-45 mmHg in infants/young children and 50-60 mmHg in adolescents, avoiding both hypoperfusion and hyperemic hyperemia.
mustKnow.source: Pediatric Brain Trauma Foundation Guidelines (Pediatr Crit Care Med 2019)

mustKnow.fact: The pediatric critical ICP threshold is 20 mmHg; sustained elevations above 20 mmHg for > 5 minutes mandate immediate escalation of tiered ICP therapies.

Tier-1 measures comprise head elevation to 30 degrees in midline, adequate sedation/analgesia, normothermia (36-37°C), normocapnia (PaCO2 35-40 mmHg), and CSF drainage via external ventricular drain (EVD).
Hypertonic 3% saline (2-5 mL/kg bolus, continuous infusion targeting serum sodium 150-155 mEq/L and osmolarity < 360 mOsm/L) is preferred over mannitol in unstable or hypotensive pediatric patients.

Prophylactic aggressive hyperventilation (PaCO2 < 30 mmHg) causes profound cerebral vasoconstriction and worsens secondary cerebral ischemia; brief hyperventilation is restricted strictly to acute brain herniation crises.

For refractory intracranial hypertension, tier-2 options include neuromuscular blockade, high-dose barbiturate infusion (pentobarbital targeting burst suppression), decompressive craniectomy, and mild hypothermia (32-34°C).

Intravenous levetiracetam (20-30 mg/kg/day) or fosphenytoin (15-20 mg PE/kg) is administered for 7 days post-injury to prevent early post-traumatic seizures; routine prophylaxis beyond 7 days is not recommended.
